turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: I suppose, Mr. Worthing, that you have some explanation for this... arrangement with Lady Bloxham?

turns.speaker: Jack
turns.text: I'm not sure I understand what you're getting at, Lady Bracknell. I was a ward of Lady Bloxham's, and she arranged for me to be adopted by my uncle, Mr. Worthing.

turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: I am not interested in your explanations, Mr. Worthing. What I want to know is what makes you think you are worthy of marrying my daughter, who is a woman of impeccable taste and breeding.

turns.speaker: Jack
turns.text: I assure you, Lady Bracknell, I am not worthy of your daughter, and I'm not sure I'm worthy of myself, either.

turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: I must say, Mr. Worthing, your lack of confidence in yourself is quite... distressing. It does little to alleviate my concerns about your suitability as a husband for my daughter.

turns.speaker: Gwendolen
turns.text: I refuse to be judged solely on the basis of your approval, Lady Bracknell. I know what I want, and I want Jack. Nothing you say will change my mind.

turns.speaker: Jack
turns.text: I don't know what to say, Lady Bracknell. I suppose I was hoping that my relationship with Gwendolen would speak for itself.

turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: I must say, Mr. Worthing, your vacillating nature is most unappealing. I fear for the stability of my daughter's future, were she to marry a man such as you.

turns.speaker: Jack
turns.text: I'm afraid I'm not quite sure what you're looking for in a son-in-law, Lady Bracknell. I'm just a simple man trying to do the right thing by Gwendolen, and I hope that's enough.

turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: I must insist, Mr. Worthing, that you provide me with some tangible proof of your identity and background. This... vagueness of yours is most unsettling.

turns.speaker: Gwendolen
turns.text: How dare you, Mother, imply that I'm not worthy of marrying Jack simply because you don't approve of him!

turns.speaker: Jack
turns.text: I'm afraid I don't have any documents or papers to prove who I am, Lady Bracknell. I'm a bit of a simple soul, and I never thought to keep such things.

turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: I must say, Mr. Worthing, your inability to produce even the most basic documentation of your identity is a grave concern. It suggests a lack of accountability and responsibility, qualities that I fear are essential in a husband for my daughter.

turns.speaker: Gwendolen
turns.text: Mother, you're being absurd! I know Jack's identity better than you ever could, and I won't have you questioning my judgment like this!

turns.speaker: Jack
turns.text: I assure you, Lady Bracknell, that I'm not trying to deceive you or hide anything. I've just never really thought about such formalities, and I'm not sure I understand why they're so important.

turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: I must insist that you take this matter seriously, Mr. Worthing. A man without a past, without a record, is a man without a future. I will not have my daughter marry someone who is, in effect, a cipher.

turns.speaker: Jack
turns.text: I'm afraid I don't mean to be a cipher, Lady Bracknell. I assure you, I do have a past, even if it is a rather...unconventional one.

turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: I must say, I am beginning to suspect that you are not the man you claim to be, Mr. Worthing. Your lack of candor and your evasive answers only serve to deepen my concerns.

turns.speaker: Gwendolen
turns.text: I won't stand for this, Mother! I know what I'm doing, and I won't be lectured to by you like some sort of naive schoolgirl!

turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: I refuse to be lectured to by my own daughter, Gwendolen. You, Mr. Worthing, have made a grave mistake in involving yourself in my family's affairs.

opening.speaker: Gwendolen
opening.text: I am engaged to Mr. Worthing, mamma.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: Pardon me, you are not engaged to any one. When you do become engaged to some one, I, or your father, should his health permit him, will inform you of the fact. An engagement should come on a young girl as a surprise, pleasant or unpleasant, as the case may be. It is hardly a matter that she could be allowed to arrange for herself . . . And now I have a few questions to put to you, Mr. Worthing. While I am making these inquiries, you, Gwendolen, will wait for me below in the carriage.

opening.speaker: Gwendolen
opening.text: Mamma!

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: In the carriage, Gwendolen!

opening.speaker: Gwendolen
opening.text: Yes, mamma.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: You can take a seat, Mr. Worthing.

opening.speaker: Jack
opening.text: Thank you, Lady Bracknell, I prefer standing.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: I feel bound to tell you that you are not down on my list of eligible young men, although I have the same list as the dear Duchess of Bolton has. We work together, in fact. However, I am quite ready to enter your name, should your answers be what a really affectionate mother requires. Do you smoke?

opening.speaker: Jack
opening.text: Well, yes, I must admit I smoke.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: I am glad to hear it. A man should always have an occupation of some kind. There are far too many idle men in London as it is. How old are you?

opening.speaker: Jack
opening.text: Twenty-nine.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: A very good age to be married at. I have always been of opinion that a man who desires to get married should know either everything or nothing. Which do you know?

opening.speaker: Jack
opening.text: I know nothing, Lady Bracknell.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: I am pleased to hear it. I do not approve of anything that tampers with natural ignorance. Ignorance is like a delicate exotic fruit; touch it and the bloom is gone. The whole theory of modern education is radically unsound. Fortunately in England, at any rate, education produces no effect whatsoever. If it did, it would prove a serious danger to the upper classes, and probably lead to acts of violence in Grosvenor Square. What is your income?

opening.speaker: Jack
opening.text: Between seven and eight thousand a year.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: In land, or in investments?

opening.speaker: Jack
opening.text: In investments, chiefly.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: That is satisfactory. What between the duties expected of one during one’s lifetime, and the duties exacted from one after one’s death, land has ceased to be either a profit or a pleasure. It gives one position, and prevents one from keeping it up. That’s all that can be said about land.

opening.speaker: Jack
opening.text: I have a country house with some land, of course, attached to it, about fifteen hundred acres, I believe; but I don’t depend on that for my real income. In fact, as far as I can make out, the poachers are the only people who make anything out of it.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: A country house! How many bedrooms? Well, that point can be cleared up afterwards. You have a town house, I hope? A girl with a simple, unspoiled nature, like Gwendolen, could hardly be expected to reside in the country.

opening.speaker: Jack
opening.text: Well, I own a house in Belgrave Square, but it is let by the year to Lady Bloxham. Of course, I can get it back whenever I like, at six months’ notice.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: Lady Bloxham? I don’t know her.

opening.speaker: Jack
opening.text: Oh, she goes about very little. She is a lady considerably advanced in years.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: Ah, nowadays that is no guarantee of respectability of character. What number in Belgrave Square?
